conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: CountertrendOnlyAfterPriorStrengthNearMagnet
candidates.quote: When a market is trending toward a magnet, it is prudent to trade with the trend until the magnet is tested and preferably overshot. Do not trade countertrend at the magnet unless there has been some prior countertrend strength like a trend line break, or unless the move is a pullback in a higher time frame trend.
candidates.description: Filter, generalized from R08-15: at any magnet level, permit a countertrend entry only if there was prior countertrend strength (e.g. an earlier trend-line break) or the move is itself a pullback within a higher-time-frame trend.

complexity.reason: 'magnet level' is generic across the many families listed in this chapter, and 'higher time frame trend' needs a design decision

notes: Umbrella restatement of R08-15 applied to every magnet type in this chapter, not just the measured-move target.

candidates.name: TrendLineRetestMagnet
candidates.description: A drawn trend line (through the two most recent swing lows in a bull trend) is a magnet: price is often drawn back to test it before the trend resumes or breaks.
candidates.pseudocode: trendLine = line through last two swing lows (pivotStrength); low[0] <= trendLine[0] + toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (level construction; trade the bounce or the break)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and trend-line projection

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineRetestMagnet
candidates.description: A trend channel line (parallel to the trend line, drawn through the extreme swing on the trend side) is a magnet: price is often drawn to test it, marking possible exhaustion.
candidates.pseudocode: channelLine = line through the trend-side pivot, parallel to the opposing trend line; high[0] >= channelLine[0] - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (level construction; fade or ride the touch)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and parallel-line projection

candidates.name: SpikeChannelStartRetest
candidates.quote: Spike and channel: the start of the channel is usually tested before long.
candidates.description: After a spike-into-channel trend transition, the bar where the channel began (the first bar after the spike's momentum eased) is a magnet the market usually retests.
candidates.pseudocode: channelStartLevel = close[c] where bar c is the identified spike-to-channel transition bar; low[0] <= channelStartLevel + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: spike-vs-channel classification is pattern recognition over a variable-length window

candidates.name: PriorSessionHighLowOpenCloseMagnet
candidates.quote: High, low, open, and close of yesterday.
candidates.description: Yesterday's session high, low, open, and close act as magnets/targets for the current session's price.
candidates.pseudocode: priorHigh = high of the prior session; priorLow = low of the prior session; priorOpen = open of the prior session; priorClose = close of the prior session; high[0] >= priorHigh - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs session/day-boundary tracking to fix yesterday's four prices

candidates.name: RecentSwingExtremeMagnet
candidates.quote: Swing highs and lows of the past few bars or even days, often setting up double bottom bull flags and double top bear flags.
candidates.description: A recent swing high or low (within the last N bars/days) is a magnet the market is often drawn back to test, frequently forming a double top or double bottom there.
candidates.pseudocode: swingLevel = highest(high, lookback)[1] (or lowest(low, lookback)[1] for the mirror); high[0] >= swingLevel - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: a highest/lowest window is enough as a proxy for a recent swing extreme

notes: Overlaps with the double top / double bottom family formalized in Chapter 12; dedup pass should merge.

candidates.name: EarlierBreakoutPointRetest
candidates.description: An earlier breakout point (the level a trend broke out above/below) remains a magnet the market is often drawn back to retest.
candidates.pseudocode: breakoutPoint = highest(high, lookback)[k] (the remembered level from BreakoutAboveSwingHigh); low[0] <= breakoutPoint + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs the remembered breakout point of a prior leg

notes: Same construction as R08-17's CountertrendTargetAtBreakoutPoint, generalized beyond the measured-move context.

candidates.name: OwnEntryPriceRetest
candidates.description: The trader's own entry price is itself a magnet -- price commonly returns to test it, a natural place to move a stop to breakeven or add to a position.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (management trigger, e.g. move stop to breakeven)

candidates.name: GapFillRetestMagnet
candidates.quote: Gaps of any kind, including moving average gaps.
candidates.description: A price gap (a true gap between bars, or a moving-average gap bar) is a magnet: the market is often drawn back to fill/retest it later.
candidates.pseudocode: gapLevel = low[g] (the top of a GapUpBar g); low[0] <= gapLevel + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the gap's boundary must persist from the bar where it formed

candidates.name: PriorTradingRangeExtremesAndMidpointMagnet
candidates.quote: Trading ranges from earlier in the day or prior days, including tight trading ranges and barbwire: the extremes and the middle often get tested. The approximate middle of the range on a trading range day, especially if there is an intraday trading range in that area (a fat area).
candidates.description: The top, bottom, and approximate middle of an earlier trading range (today's or a prior day's, including tight ranges/barbwire) are frequently retested; a secondary intraday range inside the middle (a 'fat area') is watched especially closely.
candidates.pseudocode: rangeHigh = highest(high, rangeLookback); rangeLow = lowest(low, rangeLookback); rangeMid = (rangeHigh + rangeLow) / 2; abs(close[0] - rangeMid) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize  (or close[0] near rangeHigh / rangeLow)

complexity.reason: identifying 'a trading range' at all (vs. a trend) needs a design decision, as does distinguishing barbwire from an ordinary range

candidates.name: FinalFlagRetestThenOppositeBreakout
candidates.quote: Final flags: after the breakout from the flag, the market comes back to the flag and usually breaks out of the other side.
candidates.description: After a breakout from a final flag, price commonly returns to retest the flag and then breaks out through its opposite side -- a reversal signal.
candidates.pseudocode: priorFinalFlagBreakout[k] && low[0] <= flagLow + toleranceTicks * tickSize && close[0] < flagLow
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop below the flag low (mirrored for the long case)

complexity.reason: depends on final-flag pattern recognition (R08-28) plus a retest-and-reverse test

candidates.name: NotableBarOppositeExtreme
candidates.quote: Entry bar and signal bar protective stops. Entry price (breakout test). Huge trend bar opposite extreme (the low of a huge bull trend bar and the high of a huge bear trend bar).
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the opposite extreme of a recent notable bar (a huge/large trend bar, or a signal/entry bar) is where protective stops commonly rest and therefore a magnet in its own right.
candidates.pseudocode: extreme = low[k] where bar k is a recorded LargeTrendBar (bull) within recentBars; the level persists until tested

complexity.reason: records one extreme off an already-classified bar and keeps it live for a window

candidates.name: StopRunPastNotableBarExtremeThenReverse
candidates.quote: It is fairly common for the market to work its way to those stops and then reverse back in the direction of the trend bar. ... The market reversed down off the bear inside bar that followed and formed a higher low, but not before running the protective stops below the low of the trend bar.
candidates.description: The market probes a few ticks past a NotableBarOppositeExtreme (running the protective stops resting there) and then closes back on the trend side of it -- a with-trend re-entry signal.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < extreme - runTicks * tickSize && close[0] > extreme
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the bar that closed back above the extreme (a bull reversal bar)

complexity.reason: needs the persisted notable-bar extreme plus a probe-and-close-back test

notes: Figure 10.1: bar 2 ran the stops below bar 1's low (a huge bull trend bar) and then reversed the market back up.

candidates.name: FixedTickOrDollarProfitTarget
candidates.quote: Common profit targets for scalp and swing positions: in AAPL, 50 cents and a dollar; in the 5 minute Emini, five to six ticks for a four-tick scalp, and three, four, and 10 points for a swing.
candidates.description: Exit when open profit reaches a fixed tick/dollar amount -- a small target for a scalp, a larger one for a swing.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the fixed target
notes: Instrument-specific tick counts (Emini) vs. dollar amounts (AAPL) are both folded into one dollar-denominated parameter, matching how TakeProfit is expressed in the catalog.

candidates.name: StopDistanceEqualsTargetDistance
candidates.quote: A move equal to the size of the required protective stop: if an Emini trade required you to use a 12-tick protective stop to avoid getting stopped out, expect the move to ultimately reach 12 ticks in your favor.
candidates.description: Exit target set at the same distance (in ticks) as the trade's initial protective stop, scaled by a multiple.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at entry price plus the stop distance

complexity.reason: a fixed offset from the entry price

notes: stopDistanceTicks is a parameter here since the actual protective stop is signal-bar-dependent and set per placement; related to TakeProfitWithRatioStop but framed as a 1R target rather than a dollar amount.

candidates.name: HigherTimeframeSwingAndMaMagnet
candidates.quote: Daily, weekly, and monthly swing highs and lows, bar highs and lows, moving averages, gaps, Fibonacci retracements and extensions, and trend lines.
candidates.description: Swing highs/lows, bar extremes, moving averages, gaps, and trend lines computed on a higher time frame (daily/weekly/monthly) of the same instrument act as magnets for the traded time frame.
candidates.pseudocode: higherTfLevel = swing/MA/gap/trend-line level computed on a resampled higher-timeframe series of the same instrument; abs(close[0] - higherTfLevel) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs a design decision on whether/how the engine exposes a resampled higher-timeframe data series

candidates.name: FibonacciRetracementMagnet
candidates.quote: Daily, weekly, and monthly swing highs and lows, bar highs and lows, moving averages, gaps, Fibonacci retracements and extensions, and trend lines.
candidates.description: Fibonacci retracement/extension levels (e.g. 50%, 61.8%, 127%, 161.8%) of the most recent swing act as magnets for pullbacks and projections.
candidates.pseudocode: swingHigh = highest(high, lookback)[1]; swingLow = lowest(low, lookback)[1]; fibLevel = swingHigh - fibRatio * (swingHigh - swingLow); abs(close[0] - fibLevel) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to anchor the ratio

notes: Kept separate from R10-16 because the ratio arithmetic, not just data availability, is the extra piece here.

candidates.name: RoundNumberMagnet
candidates.quote: Round numbers like hundreds in stocks (e.g., AAPL at $300) and thousands in the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow 12,000). If a stock quickly moves from $50 to $88, it will likely try to test $100 and usually go to $105 or $110 before pulling back.
candidates.description: Round-number price levels (multiples of roundStep) act as magnets; price is often drawn to the nearest one and may overshoot slightly beyond it before pulling back.
candidates.pseudocode: nearestRound = round(close[0] / roundStep) * roundStep; abs(close[0] - nearestRound) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (level construction; take profits into it or expect a slight overshoot)

complexity.reason: modular price arithmetic, no window needed

notes: roundStep is instrument-specific (100 for a $300 stock, 1000 for the Dow).

rejected.reason: a bare repeat of the tight-trading-range/barbwire item already covered by R10-10; not an independent condition

chapter_summary: An enumerated checklist of price levels ('magnets') besides gaps and measured moves that the market tends to be drawn to and test: trend lines and channel lines, spike-and-channel starts, prior-session OHLC, recent swing extremes, breakout points, entry prices, gap fills, trading-range extremes/midpoints, final flags, stop-running past notable-bar extremes, fixed tick/dollar targets, stop-distance-equals-target, higher-timeframe levels, Fibonacci levels, and round numbers. Most candidates are Exit-role target definitions of `hard`/`research` grade (they need a persisted level from pattern detection); a few (own entry price, fixed-dollar target, round numbers, stop-distance target) are trivial. R10-01 generalizes R08-15's countertrend gating to every magnet type here.
